report.source_text: Cone beam computed tomography was performed for a more detailed assessment. Figure 2a and b show an expansive mass affecting the posterior region of the right maxilla, extending to the base of the maxillary sinus. The lesion shows heterogeneous areas with varying density, suggesting mixed lytic and sclerotic components, characteristic of aggressive lesions. The presence of bone destruction is evident, with compromised bone margins and involvement of adjacent structures, indicating invasive behavior of the mass. The mass is also visible in Fig. 2c and d, causing alterations to the bone contour and invading adjacent tissues. Significant erosion of the right maxillary bone can be seen, with areas of mixed density. The irregular density of the tumor suggests the production of osteoid matrix. The extension of the lesion beyond the primary bone structures reinforces the aggressive and infiltrative nature of the lesion.

report.source_text: The slides stained with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) (Fig. 6) show the classic characteristics of a small cell osteosarcoma lesion, as evidenced by the cellular and stromal pattern. There is an intense proliferation of small, round cells with a monotonous appearance, distributed in a dense and disorganized manner. These cells have a hyperchromatic nucleus and scarce cytoplasm, reinforcing the undifferentiated nature of the neoplasm. In addition, there are areas where the stroma is mineralized, with the presence of irregularly arranged bone matrix formation, a fundamental feature for the diagnosis of osteosarcoma, as it indicates direct production of osteoid matrix by the tumour cells.

report.source_text: The immunohistochemical slides of beta-catenin (Fig. 5) show staining located predominantly in the cytoplasm of the tumor cells, with no evidence of nuclear translocation. The cytoplasmic expression of beta-catenin, with no nuclear presence, suggests the absence of activation of the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, a relevant characteristic for the differential diagnosis of tumors where this pathway is not active. CD99, on the other hand, shows strong membrane expression in tumor cells. Membrane marking of CD99 is indicative of a characteristic profile in neoplasms that present this protein, and is a relevant finding for identifying lineage-specific or aggressive tumors.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 8-year-old female presented with progressive edema, discomfort, and difficulty chewing in the right maxillofacial region. Physical examination revealed significant facial asymmetry and intraoral swelling. Initial CT imaging showed an aggressive, expansive mass in the posterior right maxilla with mixed lytic and sclerotic components, bone destruction, and irregular density suggesting osteoid matrix production. An incisional biopsy was performed due to suspicion of malignancy. Subsequently, surgical resection of the tumor was carried out. Histopathological examination of the resected tissue confirmed small cell osteosarcoma, characterized by intense proliferation of small, round cells and direct production of osteoid matrix. Immunohistochemistry showed cytoplasmic beta-catenin expression (no nuclear translocation) and strong membrane CD99 expression.

Surgical intervention involved careful removal of compromised tumor tissue with a safety margin to restore functionality and aesthetics.

Immunohistochemistry showed cytoplasmic beta-catenin expression (without nuclear translocation) and strong membrane CD99 expression in tumor cells.
